facts.claim: "Cursing Concrete" is track 2 on the 2005 No Idea Records album Rumbleseat Is Dead (3:02).
The song is credited as written by Charles Allen Ragan (Chuck Ragan).
The album was recorded at Goldentone Studios, with Rob McGregor credited as recording engineer and Michael Sarsfield as mastering engineer.
A Discogs release note says the album material was recorded at Goldentone Studios between summer 1998 and sometime in 1999.
Goldentone Studios is a recording studio in Gainesville, Florida, operated by Rob McGregor.
Rumbleseat were Chris Wollard and Chuck Ragan on guitars and vocals, and Samantha Jones on bass and vocals.
The CD edition also includes a demo version of "Cursing Concrete" (3:14), and a hidden-track version appears on streaming listings.

Rumbleseat Is Dead is the band's only full-length album. It collects songs from four 7-inch singles, two compilation tracks and four previously unreleased songs, and was released July 12, 2005 after repeated delays.
Rumbleseat was an acoustic side project of Hot Water Music's Chuck Ragan and Chris Wollard, formed in Gainesville, Florida in 1998 with Samantha Jones.
Punknews described the band as 'acoustic whiskey-influenced campfire punk rock' and noted fans waited over two years for the album.

research.lineage: Rumbleseat sits in the Gainesville, Florida punk scene around No Idea Records, as an acoustic folk and country-leaning side project of Hot Water Music members, drawing on Johnny Cash and Uncle Tupelo-style Southern acoustic songwriting.

draft:
**Cursing Concrete** starts with a man swearing at the ground. "I cursed concrete," the song admits, and on the second pass the target widens to the streets that run under his feet. It's a small, almost comic picture of anger with nowhere to go: you can shout at pavement all day and it won't move. Rumbleseat take that helplessness seriously. The song never pretends the cursing fixes anything.

What sits underneath is heavier. The narrator talks about wearing out his voice trying to lift a burden that "eats at" him, then asks a question with no answer, "Where's shame?", from a place pinned down in one hard line: "Shouting from a lot where the kids can't play." That's a dead space, a patch of ground meant for something and used for nothing, and the narrator is standing in it, loud. Then comes the walk back, replaying how things could have gone. Regret and defiance share the same few bars, and neither wins.

The turn is the hope. Wanting to "make a mark" and "stand strong even when I'm gone" moves the song from a bad night to a whole life, and the middle section says it outright: before he's done, before he lays down. The best knot in the lyric is the promise to go off but still be on. That means losing it and staying present at once. It's the voice of someone who knows his temper and has decided to keep showing up anyway.

The band plays it like a push forward. A strummed acoustic guitar drives at a medium-fast clip, a distorted electric holds long chords over it, the bass walks instead of sitting on the root, and the snare cracks hard. The voices come doubled, moving together in unison or close parallel lines, so the confession sounds shared, like a room singing along. The arrangement doesn't build or pull back. It just keeps going, which suits a song about not stopping. The mix is clean, with the electric guitar's grit as its rough edge.

Chuck Ragan wrote it. Rumbleseat was the acoustic side project he and Chris Wollard ran outside Hot Water Music, formed in Gainesville in 1998 with Samantha Jones on bass and vocals, all three singing. Punknews called them "acoustic whiskey-influenced campfire punk rock," which gets the Johnny Cash and Uncle Tupelo lean right. The song was cut at Rob McGregor's Goldentone Studios in Gainesville around 1998 and 1999, and it waited until 2005 to land on the band's only full-length, an album titled like an obituary. That suits a song so worried about leaving a mark after it's gone.

It sticks because it lets you be furious and hopeful in the same breath, and it hands you a chorus to shout at the pavement with a few friends.

factCheck.claim: "I cursed concrete" is a lyric, and the target later widens to the streets that run under the narrator's feet.
factCheck.note: The quote matches the lyrics and the streets line is there. 'On the second pass' was reworded to 'later' because it could be read as a reference to the listening passes. 'His feet' was made neutral because the lyrics give no gender.

factCheck.claim: The narrator is a man ('a man swearing', 'his voice', 'his temper', 'he').
factCheck.note: The lyrics don't state the narrator's gender, and only one listening pass said 'male voice'. Pronouns were made neutral.

factCheck.claim: Quoted fragments "eats at", "Where's shame?", "make a mark", plus the other quoted lines.
factCheck.note: The fragments match the lyrics, but the draft quoted more than three lines in total. The quotes were trimmed to three, and the rest were paraphrased.
